questions.question: Which type of mercury in food should I actually worry about?
questions.answer: Methylmercury (MeHg) is the form relevant to dietary risk, and it comes primarily from fish and seafood, especially long-lived predatory fish ([[sources/atsdr-mercury-toxprofile-2024|ATSDR 2024]]). Inorganic mercury exposure through diet is uncommon, and elemental mercury vapor from dental amalgam is a separate exposure handled through dental practice rather than food choice ([[sources/atsdr-mercury-toxprofile-2024|ATSDR 2024]]).

questions.question: Which fish are highest in mercury and which are safest to eat?
questions.answer: Long-lived predatory fish such as swordfish, shark, king mackerel, tilefish, bigeye tuna, marlin, and orange roughy carry methylmercury roughly 10x to 50x higher than lower-trophic-level fish and are in the FDA/EPA "Choices to Avoid" category ([[sources/fda-epa-fish-consumption-advice|FDA/EPA Fish Advice]]). Lower-mercury "Best Choices" like salmon, sardines, anchovies, tilapia, shrimp, and catfish (under 0.1 ppm) are recommended at 2 to 3 servings per week, while light canned tuna is a "Good Choice" at 1 serving per week ([[sources/fda-epa-fish-consumption-advice|FDA/EPA Fish Advice]]).

questions.question: Why are pregnant women and children singled out for mercury advice?
questions.answer: Methylmercury crosses the placenta and concentrates in the developing fetal brain, and the developmental window is the most consequential exposure period ([[sources/farina-rocha-aschner-2011-mehg-mechanism|Farina et al. 2011]]). The major dietary reference values from EFSA, JECFA, and EPA IRIS are all anchored on developmental neurotoxicity, so pregnant and breastfeeding women, women who might become pregnant, and children should follow the FDA/EPA fish categories rather than averaging across "fish" as one group ([[sources/efsa-mercury-methylmercury-2012|EFSA 2012]], [[sources/jecfa-61st-methylmercury|JECFA 61st]], [[sources/fda-epa-fish-consumption-advice|FDA/EPA Fish Advice]]).

questions.question: What are the official regulatory limits for methylmercury?
questions.answer: The main dietary reference values are the EPA IRIS oral RfD of 0.1 µg/kg/day, the EFSA tolerable weekly intake (TWI) of 1.3 µg Hg/kg body weight per week (daily equivalent about 0.19), and the JECFA provisional tolerable weekly intake (PTWI) of 1.6 µg/kg body weight per week (daily equivalent about 0.23) ([[sources/epa-iris-methylmercury|EPA IRIS MeHg]], [[sources/efsa-mercury-methylmercury-2012|EFSA 2012]], [[sources/jecfa-61st-methylmercury|JECFA 61st]]). These values agree to within a factor of 2.3, making mercury the most regulatory-harmonized of the heavy metals on this wiki, and all are anchored on the same Faroe Islands and Seychelles cohort developmental-neurotoxicity endpoint ([[sources/efsa-mercury-methylmercury-2012|EFSA 2012]]).

questions.question: How is mercury exposure measured in people?
questions.answer: Biomonitoring for methylmercury exposure typically measures hair mercury, which integrates exposure over weeks to months, or whole-blood mercury, which reflects recent integrated exposure ([[sources/jecfa-61st-methylmercury|JECFA 61st]], [[sources/efsa-mercury-methylmercury-2012|EFSA 2012]]). Maternal hair mercury was the dominant biomarker in the Faroe Islands cohort that underlies the EFSA TWI ([[sources/efsa-mercury-methylmercury-2012|EFSA 2012]]).

questions.question: How much light canned tuna can I safely eat?
questions.answer: Light canned tuna contains roughly 0.1 to 0.3 ppm methylmercury, so a 100-gram serving delivers about 10 to 30 µg ([[sources/fda-epa-fish-consumption-advice|FDA/EPA Fish Advice]]). For a 70-kg adult, one can per week is at or below the EFSA TWI, but for a 25-kg child a single serving would be at or above all three reference values, which is why the FDA/EPA "Good Choices" guidance of 1 serving per week with age-scaled serving sizes exists ([[sources/fda-epa-fish-consumption-advice|FDA/EPA Fish Advice]]).
